unit.title: Use and maintain hand and power tools for electrical work

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which tool is made to remove the insulation from the end of a conductor without damaging the copper?

Tightening the terminal screws in a socket

questions.stem: How should you hold a small piece of metal that you are drilling with a power drill?

questions.stem: Why is a light film of oil put on the joint of pliers and cutters?

questions.stem: What should you do with a hacksaw blade that has missing teeth?

questions.stem: How should the battery of a cordless drill be looked after?

questions.stem: Where is the best place to store hand tools at the end of the day?

questions.stem: Why is it unsafe to carry sharp tools in your trouser pocket?

essays.stem: You are to fit and connect a new socket outlet on a dead, isolated circuit. List the hand tools you would use and say what each one is for.
essays.modelAnswer: After the circuit has been isolated and proved dead, I would use a tape measure and a pencil to mark the height of the box, and a spirit level to keep it straight. A cordless drill with a masonry bit makes the holes for wall plugs in the block wall, and a screwdriver of the right size fixes the box. A utility knife or a cable sheath stripper takes off the outer sheath, cutting away from my body. Side cutters cut the conductors to length, and wire strippers, set to the right size, remove the insulation without nicking the copper. Long-nose pliers help me shape the conductors to fit the terminals. An insulated screwdriver of the right size tightens the terminal screws firmly, and I check each one with a gentle pull. Finally I use a spirit level again to set the faceplate straight before tightening its screws.
markingPoints: Tape measure and spirit level to mark and level the box
Drill with masonry bit, wall plugs and a correctly sized screwdriver to fix the box
Knife or sheath stripper and side cutters to prepare the cable
Wire strippers set to size so the copper is not nicked; pliers to shape conductors
Insulated screwdriver to tighten terminals, then a pull test and levelling of the faceplate

essays.stem: Describe how to drill a hole safely in a concrete block wall with a hammer drill.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the drill, its lead and plug for damage, and I make sure the supply is RCD-protected, or I use a battery drill. I check the wall for hidden cables and pipes with a detector and look for boxes or switches nearby, and I do not drill in line above or below them. I mark the spot and put on safety glasses, a dust mask and ear protection. With the drill unplugged, I fit a masonry bit of the right size firmly in the chuck and remove the chuck key. I set the drill to hammer action and fit the side handle. I hold the drill with both hands, square to the wall, and start slowly to stop the bit wandering. I let the drill do the work and pull it back now and then to clear the dust. When done, I unplug the drill, let the bit cool and clean up the dust.
markingPoints: Checks the drill, lead and plug; uses an RCD-protected supply or a battery drill
Checks the wall for hidden cables and pipes before drilling
Wears safety glasses, a dust mask and ear protection
Fits a masonry bit with the drill unplugged; removes the chuck key; uses hammer setting and side handle
Holds the drill with both hands, starts slowly, lets the drill do the work, clears dust and cleans up

essays.stem: Explain the checks you should make on a mains power tool and its extension lead before use, and why each check matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I look along the whole lead for cuts, crushing or tape repairs, because damaged insulation can expose live copper and cause a shock. I check that the outer sheath is gripped where it enters the plug and the tool, so the conductors cannot be pulled loose. I check the plug for cracks, burns and bent pins, because burns show overheating and loose connections. I look at the tool casing for cracks, because a broken case can let a person touch live parts. I check that guards are fitted and work, and that the switch turns the tool on and off properly, so the tool cannot run when I do not want it to. I check that the extension lead is rated for the tool and is fully unwound, so that it does not overheat. If anything is wrong, I do not use it: I tag it and report it.
markingPoints: Checks the lead for cuts or repairs, and says this prevents shock
Checks that the sheath is gripped at the plug and the tool
Checks the plug and casing for cracks or burns, which show damage or overheating
Checks guards and the on-off switch work properly
Checks the extension lead rating and unwinds it; tags and reports faulty items

essays.stem: Describe how you would care for and maintain your set of electrical hand tools.
essays.modelAnswer: At the end of each job I wipe my tools clean of dust, plaster and grease with a dry cloth, and I dry them if they get wet, so they do not rust. I put a drop of light oil on the joints of pliers and cutters and work them open and shut, then wipe off the extra oil so that the handles are not slippery. I check that cutting edges are sharp and that the jaws meet properly. I replace hacksaw blades that are blunt or have missing teeth, and knife blades that are dull. I check the insulated handles of screwdrivers and pliers for cracks, cuts or worn spots; any insulated tool that is damaged is taken out of use and replaced, not taped. I keep my tools in a dry, lockable toolbox with a place for each one, so that they are not damaged and I can see if anything is missing.
markingPoints: Cleans and dries tools after use to stop rust
Lightly oils joints and wipes off the extra
Keeps cutting edges sharp; replaces blunt or damaged blades
Checks insulated handles and replaces damaged insulated tools (never tapes them)
Stores tools dry and organised in a lockable box

essays.stem: Explain why electricians use insulated hand tools, how they should be checked, and why they do not make live work safe.
essays.modelAnswer: Insulated tools, such as screwdrivers and pliers with insulated handles and shafts, are marked with a voltage rating. They give an extra layer of protection if a conductor that should be dead turns out to be live, for example because of a wrong label or someone else's mistake. Before each use I check the insulation for cracks, cuts, burns, worn spots or bare metal showing where it should be covered. If I find damage, the tool must be taken out of use and replaced, because tape will not restore its protection. Insulated tools do not make it safe to work live. The insulation can be damaged without being seen, and a slip can bring a hand, arm or another tool onto a live part. Working live can also cause an arc flash. The safe way is always to isolate the circuit, lock it off, tag it and prove it dead first.
markingPoints: Insulated tools carry a voltage rating and protect against accidental contact
Checks for cracks, cuts, burns or bare metal before use
Damaged insulated tools are replaced, not taped
Insulation can fail and a slip can still cause contact or an arc flash
States the safe method: isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead; never work live

essays.stem: Compare a cordless (battery) drill and a mains (corded) drill for electrical work on a building site.
essays.modelAnswer: A cordless drill runs on a rechargeable battery. It has no mains lead, so there is nothing to trip over, cut or damage, and no risk of a shock from a damaged lead. It is easy to carry up ladders and into ceilings, and it can be used where there is no supply yet. However, the battery runs down and must be charged, so a spare battery is useful, and many cordless drills are less powerful for large holes in concrete. A mains drill is usually more powerful and keeps going all day without charging, which suits heavy drilling in block and concrete. But it needs a supply, a lead and often an extension lead, which must be checked and protected by an RCD, and the lead can be a trip hazard. On most sites a cordless drill is chosen for general fixing and a mains hammer drill for heavy work.
markingPoints: Cordless: no lead, so fewer trip and shock hazards, and easy to carry
Cordless: battery needs charging and may have less power
Mains: more power and runs all day without charging
Mains: needs a checked lead, RCD protection, and the lead is a trip hazard
Gives a sensible choice for each kind of work

essays.stem: Describe how to cut, clean and bend a length of PVC conduit using hand tools.
essays.modelAnswer: I measure the length I need with a tape measure and mark it all round the conduit with a pencil, so the cut will be square. I hold the conduit firmly in a vice or on a bench hook, without crushing it. I cut it on the mark with a fine-tooth hacksaw, using steady full strokes, or with a ratchet conduit cutter. I then remove the burrs from the inside and outside of the end with a reamer, file or knife, so that they cannot damage the cables. To bend it, I push a bending spring of the right size into the conduit until it reaches the bend, tied to a string so I can pull it out. In hot weather the conduit bends easily; I bend it slowly over my knee or a form, a little past the angle I want, then let it spring back. I twist and pull out the spring and check the bend with a square.
markingPoints: Measures and marks the cut all round so it is square
Holds the conduit firmly without crushing and cuts with a fine-tooth hacksaw or conduit cutter
Deburrs the cut end inside and out so cables are not damaged
Uses a bending spring of the correct size, on a string, to stop kinking
Bends slowly to the right angle, removes the spring and checks the bend

essays.stem: Explain how to use an angle grinder safely, for example to cut a steel strap or a slot in a metal enclosure.
essays.modelAnswer: Before I start, I check the grinder, lead and plug for damage, and check that the guard is fitted and set between me and the disc. I make sure the disc is the right type for cutting metal, is not cracked, and has a speed rating that suits the grinder. I change discs only with the grinder unplugged, using the proper key. I wear safety glasses with a face shield, ear protection, gloves and close-fitting clothing, and I clear away anything that can burn, because the sparks are hot. I clamp the work firmly instead of holding it in my hand. I hold the grinder with both hands, using the side handle, and let it reach full speed before cutting. I stand to the side of the disc, never in line with it. When I finish, I wait for the disc to stop before putting the grinder down, and then unplug it.
markingPoints: Checks the tool, lead and guard before use
Checks the disc type, condition and speed rating; changes discs only when unplugged
Wears eye and face protection, ear protection and gloves; removes things that can burn
Clamps the work and holds the grinder with both hands, standing out of line with the disc
Waits for the disc to stop before putting it down, then unplugs it

essays.stem: Describe how power tools, leads and batteries should be stored when they are not in use.
essays.modelAnswer: Power tools should be cleaned of dust after use and stored in their own cases, or on shelves in a dry, lockable store, so that they are not knocked, stolen or used by people who are not trained. Leads should be coiled loosely, without kinks or tight wraps around the tool, and hung up or put away so they are not crushed or left as trip hazards. Extension drums should be fully wound in when stored, kept dry and out of the sun. Battery packs should be charged only with their own charger, removed from the charger when full if the maker says so, and stored in a cool, dry place away from metal objects that could short the terminals. Batteries should not be left in a hot vehicle. Any tool or lead that is damaged should be tagged 'Do not use' and kept apart from the good ones until it is repaired.
markingPoints: Cleans tools and stores them in cases or a dry, lockable store
Coils leads loosely and stores them off the floor
Charges batteries only with their own charger, as the maker says
Stores batteries cool and dry, away from heat and metal objects
Keeps tagged, damaged tools apart from good ones

essays.stem: Explain why good housekeeping and keeping track of tools matter on an electrical job, and how you would do it.
essays.modelAnswer: Good housekeeping keeps the work area safe and helps the job go well. Tools, off-cuts and leads left on the floor can cause trips and falls, and tools left in ceilings, boards or boxes can damage cables or cause a short circuit when the supply is restored. A tidy area also shows the customer that the work is professional. To keep track, I use a toolbox with a place for each tool, or a tool list, and I count my tools at the end of each task and before any board is closed or energised. I keep leads out of walkways and coil them away when not in use. I sweep up off-cuts, dust and screws as I go and put waste in the right bin, with metal scrap and broken lamps kept apart. At the end of the day I lock the tools away and report any that are lost or damaged.
markingPoints: Explains trip and fall hazards from tools, leads and off-cuts
Explains that tools left in boards or ceilings can cause damage or short circuits
Uses a toolbox with a place for each tool or a tool list, and counts tools before energising
Clears waste as work goes on and sorts it into the right bins
Locks tools away and reports lost or damaged tools

practical1.title: Fix PVC conduit and boxes on a practice board and prepare the cable ends with hand tools
practical1.brief: As a group, use hand tools to fix a short PVC conduit run on the Centre's plywood practice board and prepare the cables for connection. The board is NOT connected to any supply. The run goes from a surface switch box to a surface socket-outlet box about 1 m away, with one 90° bend made with a bending spring. Share the stages so that every member uses the tools while the others watch and check: (1) measure, mark and level the box positions with a tape measure and spirit level, (2) fix the boxes with screws of the right size, (3) measure, mark, cut and deburr the conduit, (4) make the bend with the bending spring and fit the conduit and saddles, (5) draw the conductors in with a draw wire, (6) strip the conductor ends with wire strippers set to the right size, and fit them to the switch and outlet terminals, looped clockwise or straight as the terminal needs. In a group of 4, one member does two stages; in every case each member strips and terminates at least one conductor. Each member then tells the assessor which tools they used and why. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the board is finished and the bench is clean.
materials: Plywood practice board, about 1.2 m × 0.6 m, fixed upright (not connected to any supply)
1 surface switch box and 1 surface socket-outlet box, with a switch and a socket outlet
About 1.5 m of 20 mm PVC conduit, saddles and box connectors
Single-core insulated conductors for the run
Tape measure, pencil, spirit level, screwdrivers, fine-tooth hacksaw or conduit cutter, reamer or file, bending spring, draw wire, wire strippers, side cutters, long-nose pliers
Screws of the right size for the boxes and saddles
Safety glasses and gloves for every member
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The tools laid out and checked before starting, with every member in safety glasses
The box positions marked and checked with the spirit level
The conduit cut and deburred, showing a clean square end
The bend made with the bending spring, and the conduit fixed in its saddles
Conductor ends stripped to the right length, with no nicks
The conductors fitted in the switch and outlet terminals
The finished board and the cleaned bench, with the tools put away
checklist: Checked each tool for damage before use and chose the right tool for each step
Measured and marked accurately and used the spirit level correctly
Cut the conduit square with the hacksaw or cutter, keeping hands clear of the blade
Removed the burrs from the cut ends
Used the bending spring correctly, with no kinks in the bend
Set the wire strippers to the conductor size and stripped without nicking the copper
Fitted conductors into terminals with no bare copper showing outside and tightened them firmly
Explained to the assessor which tools they used and why
Cleaned the tools and returned them to their places
safety: This board must not be connected to any supply during the task
Wear safety glasses when cutting and stripping; cut away from your body and keep fingers clear of blades
Hold the conduit firmly in a vice or bench hook while cutting; never on your knee
Carry and pass tools handle first, and keep sharp tools out of your pockets
Sweep up off-cuts and stripped insulation as you go so nobody slips; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Inspect and maintain the group's toolkit, then drill and fix wall plugs in a block panel
practical2.brief: As a group, inspect, clean and maintain a kit of electrical hand and power tools, record the results, and then use a drill safely to make fixings. Part A (about 1 hour 30 minutes): each member is given part of the kit by the assessor (for example insulated screwdrivers and pliers; cutters and strippers; the hacksaw and blades; a mains drill and extension lead; a cordless drill and battery). Each member inspects their tools, cleans them, oils the joints, changes a hacksaw blade if needed, and checks leads, plugs and casings with the tools unplugged. Any tool that is faulty is tagged 'Do not use' and set apart. Every member records their checks on the group's tool register. Part B (about 1 hour): on the Centre's concrete block practice panel, which has no hidden cables, each member marks, drills and plugs two holes with the hammer drill or cordless drill and fixes a surface box with screws. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the tool register once for the whole group when the tools are stored and the area is clean.
materials: A kit of electrical hand tools (insulated screwdrivers and pliers, side cutters, wire strippers, hacksaw, utility knife)
A mains hammer drill with an extension lead, used from an RCD-protected socket, and a cordless drill with its battery and charger
Masonry bits of the right size for the wall plugs, and spare hacksaw blades
Light machine oil, clean dry cloths and a soft brush
'Do not use' tags and the group's tool register sheet
Concrete block practice panel, wall plugs, screws and surface boxes
Safety glasses, dust masks, ear protection and gloves for every member
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The full toolkit laid out on the bench before inspection
A member checking a drill lead, plug and casing with the drill unplugged
Insulated handles being checked, and a faulty item tagged 'Do not use'
Tools cleaned and oiled, with a new hacksaw blade fitted the right way
A member drilling the block panel in full PPE, holding the drill with both hands
The surface boxes fixed to the panel, one per member
The completed tool register and the tools stored back in their places
checklist: Inspected each tool given to them and found any damage correctly
Checked power tool leads, plugs and casings only with the tool unplugged
Cleaned and lightly oiled the tools and fitted a hacksaw blade with the teeth pointing away from the handle
Tagged faulty tools 'Do not use', set them apart and recorded them on the register
Wore safety glasses, a dust mask and ear protection while drilling
Fitted the masonry bit with the drill unplugged, removed the chuck key and used the correct setting
Drilled square and to the right depth, and fixed the box firmly and level
Stored the tools, coiled the leads and cleaned up the dust
safety: Unplug a power tool before you inspect it, change a bit or clean it
Use the mains drill only from an RCD-protected socket, with the extension lead fully unwound
